newsitem.title: USA: Some US economists say Fed to tighten in February.
newsitem.headline: Some US economists say Fed to tighten in February.

text.p: A few U.S. economists expect the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates next month despite recent benign inflation reports.

Most economists -- 27 of 29 in a Reuters survey -- expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged in February. But those who expect a tightening argued that the Fed can no longer ignore prolonged labor market tightness or swift demand growth.

"Given the supply side is so tight, the unemployment rate is well below what is considered full employment and wages are accelerating," said Ken Bercuson, head of economic research for the Americas at SBC Warburg.
Bercuson estimated a 70 percent likelihood the Fed will tighten at its February 4-5 policy meeting in anticipation of rising inflation.
Inflation will accelerate in the near term because growing consumer demand and rising wages will allow merchandisers to pass higher prices along to consumers, Bercuson said.

"Final demand is growing much more quickly than the Fed had hoped, and with inventory-to-sales ratios at historic lows, one would expect renewed inventory demand in the first half of this year," he said.
Although a February rate hike might surprise the financial markets, it should not be seen as particularly preemptive, Bercuson said.
"The accelerating economy is really moving along on all cylinders now," said Raphael Marrone, a money market economist at Deutshe Morgan Grenfell.
Over the past couple of weeks, Deutsche changed its view to favor a February rate hike, Marrone said.
"Now you're having some of the pipeline indicators, the leading inflation indicators, moving up," he said.
A rise in the Employment Cost Index and a surge in fourth-quarter GDP would push the Fed toward tightening, Marrone said.

Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp, said the central bank probably will not shift rates at the February meeting but added that if he had a say in the matter, he would vote for a tightening.
"A small insurance policy right now would be a very good investment," Sohn said. "The best news on inflation is behind us now; we will see higher prices down the road."
Consumer and producer price data for December were benign enough to stay the Fed's hand for now, Sohn said.
"They want proof positive that inflation is becoming a problem before they start to hike interest rates," he said, adding that "there is about a 60 percent probability" of a March tightening.
